# comparing groups {#comparing-means -}

::: {.chapter-card}

```{r fig.align='center', echo=FALSE, include=identical(knitr:::pandoc_to(), 'html'), results="markup"}
knitr:::include_graphics('https://thebustalab.github.io/integrated_bioanalytics/images/hawaii_aquifers.jpeg', dpi = NA)
```

<div class="cc-title-slot"></div>

**Are these two things the same?** Does one aquifer hold more potassium than another, did a treatment change the amount of a metabolite, or do plants from two sites differ in leaf chemistry? Some difference between two groups is expected by chance alone, so a statistical test asks how likely data as extreme as that in hand would be if the groups came from the same distribution. This chapter checks the distributions first, compares two groups with a t-test or a Wilcoxon test and more than two with Games-Howell or Dunn tests, and marks the results on a plot.

[One-page summary (PDF)](https://thebustalab.github.io/integrated_bioanalytics/summary_sheets/11_comparing_means.pdf){.cc-btn target="_blank"} [Jump to the chapter summary](#comparing-means-summary){.cc-btn .ghost}

knitr:::include_graphics('https://thebustalab.github.io/integrated_bioanalytics/images/11_comparing_means_flowchart.png', dpi = NA)

Many of the concepts discussed in this chapter are easier to think about with an example in mind. For that, suppose we are analytical chemists on Hawaii, studying the chemistry of the island's aquifers with the data set `hawaii_aquifers` in hand. The output below shows the structure of the data set: we have 990 measurements of 9 different analytes in multiple wells, each of which draws on one of 10 aquifers.

```{r}
hawaii_aquifers
unique(hawaii_aquifers$aquifer_code)
```
Importantly, there are many wells that draw on each aquifer, as shown in the graph below.

```{r, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4, fig.cap = "Number of wells drawing on each Hawaiian aquifer. Horizontal bar chart of the number of distinct wells sampled (x axis) for each of the ten aquifers (y axis); each bar is one aquifer. Every aquifer is represented by more than one well, so the wells can be treated as repeated, independent measurements of their aquifer. Data are from the 'hawaii_aquifers' dataset used in UMD CHEM5725."}
hawaii_aquifers %>%
  select(aquifer_code, well_name) %>%
  group_by(aquifer_code) %>%
  summarize(n_wells = length(unique(well_name))) -> aquifers_summarized

aquifers_summarized

ggplot(aquifers_summarized) + geom_col(aes(x = n_wells, y = aquifer_code))
```

## definitions {-}

1. **populations and independent measurements**: When we are comparing means, we are comparing two *sets* of values. It is important to consider where these values came from in the first place. In particular, it is usually useful to think of these values as representatives of larger populations. In the example of our aquifer data set, we can think of the measurements from different wells drawing on the same aquifer as independent measurements of the "population" (i.e. the aquifer).

2. **the null hypothesis**: When we conduct a statistical test, we are testing the null hypothesis. The null (think "default") hypothesis is that there is no difference between the distributions (which is where the name "null" comes from). In the example of our aquifers, let's say that we're interested in whether two aquifers have different abundances of potassium - in this case the null hypothesis is that they do not differ, in other words, that they have the same amount of potassium.

3. **the *p* value**: The *p* value represents the probability of getting data as extreme as our results if the null hypothesis is true. In other words: the *p* value is the probability that we would observe the differences in our samples that we did, if in fact there were no differences in the populations at all. To continue with our example: suppose we measure potassium levels in 10% of the wells that access each aquifer and find that aquifer_1 has potassium levels of 14 +/- 2 and aquifer_2 has potassium levels of 12 +/- 1. Suppose that we then conduct a statistical test and get a p value of 0.04. This means that, assuming the aquifers have the same potassium levels (i.e. assuming the null hypothesis is true), there is a 4% chance of getting values at least as extreme as the ones we measured. In other words, IF the aquifers have the same potassium abundance, it is pretty unlikely that we would have obtained the measurements that we did.

Please note that the *p* value is not the probability of a detected difference being a false positive. The probability of a false positive requires additional information in order to be calculated. For further discussion please see the end of this chapter.

## distributions {-}

Before comparing two means, first look at the two distributions. This initial inspection is not a formality. Every statistical test in this chapter makes assumptions about the *shape* of the data (the parametric tests assume each group is roughly normally distributed, and the rank tests assume the groups have similar shapes), and a mean on its own reveals nothing about either. Two groups can have identical means and completely different distributions, and a bar chart of the means will hide that perfectly (#barbarcharts). So, it is worth knowing how to draw a distribution in full rather than relying solely on summary statistics.

By using multiple geoms, a single plot can show the summary (mean, median, etc.), the density, and the raw observations at once. In the plot below, the half-eye gives the density, the boxplot the quartiles, and the dots every actual measurement, showing the shape, the spread and the sample size in one picture:

```{r, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4.5, fig.cap = "Highway fuel economy of cars with four, six and eight cylinders, drawn three ways at once. For each cylinder count (x axis, also encoded by fill color), the half-eye on the right shows the density of highway fuel economy (miles per gallon, y axis), the boxplot shows the median and quartiles, and the dots on the left show every individual car, one dot per car. Data are the 'mpg' dataset from the ggplot2 package (US EPA fuel economy data for 1999 and 2008 models)."}
mpg %>% filter(cyl %in% c(4,6,8)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(cyl), y = hwy, fill = factor(cyl))) +
  ggdist::stat_halfeye(
    adjust = 0.5, justification = -0.2, .width = 0, point_colour = NA
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.12, outlier.color = NA, alpha = 0.5) +
  ggdist::stat_dots(side = "left", justification = 1.1, binwidth = .25)
```

Look at what this shows that a bar chart would not: how many observations there actually are, whether the distribution is skewed, and whether any group is bimodal. All three change which statistical test would be needed to complete the work described in the next section.

## test selection {-}

When we are comparing means, we need to first determine what kind of statistical tests we can use with our data. If our data can be reasonably modeled by a normal distribution, then we can use what are called "parametric" tests. Under those conditions they are the most powerful choice, meaning they can detect smaller differences as statistically significant. If the data are not normally distributed within each group we are comparing, the p-values from parametric tests may no longer be accurate, especially with small samples, so we switch to "non-parametric" tests, whose p-values hold up regardless of the shape of the data. Non-parametric tests are not simply weaker versions of the parametric ones: with skewed data or a few outliers, they are often the more powerful choice as well.

A helpful way to think about the non-parametric tests in this chapter is that each one ranks all of the values, then does something close to its parametric partner on those ranks. The Wilcox test behaves much like a t-test run on ranks, and the Dunn test (for more than two groups) much like a set of pairwise comparisons run on ranks. This is an approximation rather than exactly what the software computes, but it explains why these tests do not need normally distributed data: ranks always run from 1 to N, whatever the measurements looked like, so a skewed distribution or an extreme value cannot distort them.

So, the first question we must answer is whether each group within our data can be sufficiently approximated using a normal distribution. We can check our data for normality using the Shapiro test. Let's use the `hawaii_aquifers` data as an example, and let's consider only the element potassium:

```{r, message = FALSE}
K_data <- hawaii_aquifers %>%
  filter(analyte == "K")
  K_data
```

To work with two means, let's just look at aquifers 1 and 6:

```{r, fig.width = 4.5, fig.height = 4, fig.cap = "Potassium in aquifers 1 and 6. Boxplots of potassium abundance (y axis) for the two aquifers (x axis), with each point one measurement from a well drawing on that aquifer; there are twelve measurements in each aquifer. Data are from the 'hawaii_aquifers' dataset used in UMD CHEM5725."}
K_data_1_6 <- K_data %>%
    filter(aquifer_code %in% c("aquifer_1", "aquifer_6"))

K_data_1_6

ggplot(K_data_1_6, aes(x = aquifer_code, y = abundance)) +
    geom_boxplot() +
    geom_point()
```

Are these data normally distributed? Let's get a first approximation by looking at a plot:

```{r, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.5, fig.cap = "Distributions of potassium in aquifers 1 and 6. Histograms (gray bars, 30 bins) of potassium abundance (x axis), one panel per aquifer, in which the height of each bar is the number of measurements in that bin. A density curve (blue line) is drawn over each histogram, multiplied by ten so that it shares the y axis with the bars, which is why that axis is labeled density * 10. With twelve measurements per aquifer, it is hard to judge by eye whether either distribution is normal. Data are from the 'hawaii_aquifers' dataset used in UMD CHEM5725."}
K_data_1_6 %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = abundance)) +
    geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
    facet_wrap(~aquifer_code) +
    geom_density(aes(y = ..density..*10), color = "blue")
```

Based on this graphic, it's hard to say! Let's use a statistical test to help. When we want to run the Shapiro test, we are looking to see if each group has normally distributed here (here group is "aquifer_code", i.e. aquifer_1 and aquifer_6). This means we need to `group_by(aquifer_code)` before we run the test:

```{r}
K_data_1_6 %>%
  group_by(aquifer_code) %>% 
  shapiroTest(abundance)
```

Both p-values are above 0.05! This means that the distributions are not significantly different from a normal distribution. What about the spread of the two groups? The t-test used in this course is Welch's t-test, which does not assume the two groups have equal variances, so for two groups there is no need to test the variances before choosing a test. (Student's t-test, the older version, does assume equal variances. It is barely more powerful when that assumption holds and can give badly misleading p-values when it does not, which is why Welch's version is the default.)

<hr>

## two means {-}

Now, since our data passed the Shapiro test, we can use a t-test. A t-test is a parametric test. This means that it relies on modeling the data using a normal distribution in order to make comparisons. When its assumptions hold, it is also the most powerful test available, meaning it is the most likely to detect a difference in means, assuming one is present. Like every test in this chapter, it takes a formula written with a tilde (`~`). The **response**, the measured value being compared, goes on the left of the tilde, and the **predictor**, here the column that sorts the measurements into groups, goes on the right. In `abundance ~ aquifer_code`, the response is `abundance` and the predictor is `aquifer_code`. The regression and ANOVA chapters use the same `response ~ predictor` form, where a predictor can also be a number. Let's try it out:

```{r}
K_data_1_6 %>%
  tTest(abundance ~ aquifer_code)
```

A p-value of 0.012! This is below 0.05, meaning that if the two aquifers truly had the same mean, we would only observe a difference at least this extreme about 1.2% of the time. That gives us fairly strong evidence that the means differ. Suppose that our data had not passed the Shapiro test. We would then need to use a Wilcox test. The Wilcox test is a non-parametric test, which means that it does not use a normal distribution to model the data in order to make comparisons. Instead, it compares the groups using the ranks of the measurements rather than the measurements themselves, so its p-value does not depend on the shape of the distribution. For fun, let's try that one out and compare the p-values from the two methods:

```{r}
K_data_1_6 %>%
  wilcoxTest(abundance ~ aquifer_code)
```

A p-value of 0.028! This is higher than the t-test's value (0.012) because the Wilcox test works with less information. Rather than the measured values themselves, it pools both groups, ranks every observation from smallest to largest, and asks whether values from one group tend to rank higher than those from the other. Its null hypothesis is that both groups come from the same distribution. If the two aquifers really had identical distributions, we would see a result this extreme only about 2.8% of the time.

Strictly speaking, then, the Wilcox test compares neither means nor medians. When the two distributions share a shape and are simply shifted relative to one another, its question reduces to whether the medians differ, which is why the median is the usual summary to report alongside a Wilcox result. When the shapes clearly do not match, still report the medians as a description, but phrase the conclusion as "values in group A tend to be higher than values in group B."

Working on ranks also makes the test resistant to outliers. A reading ten times larger than the rest still counts only as the top rank, whereas the same reading can drag a mean a long way. Ranking also means the two tests can disagree, and occasionally point in opposite directions. Consider nitrate measured in 30 soil samples from each of two orchards. Every north sample sits between 13 and 17 mg/kg. Most south samples are lower, between 8 and 12, but eight of them come from beds near a manure store and read between 80 and 120:

```{r, fig.cap = "Nitrate in soil samples from two orchards. Strip plot of nitrate concentration (mg/kg, y axis) for the north and south orchards (x axis); each point is one soil sample. Most south samples sit below every north sample, but eight very high south readings pull the south mean above the north mean. Data are a constructed teaching example.", fig.width = 4.5, fig.height = 4}
orchards <- tibble(
  orchard = rep(c("north", "south"), each = 30),
  nitrate = c(seq(13, 17, length.out = 30),
              seq(8, 12, length.out = 22), seq(80, 120, length.out = 8))
)

ggplot(orchards, aes(x = orchard, y = nitrate)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, height = 0)

orchards %>%
  group_by(orchard) %>%
  summarize(mean = mean(nitrate), median = median(nitrate))
```

The south orchard has the higher mean (34 vs 15) but the lower median (10.8 vs 15). Now both tests:

```{r}
orchards %>%
  tTest(nitrate ~ orchard)

orchards %>%
  wilcoxTest(nitrate ~ orchard)
```

Both p-values are below 0.05, and the two results point in opposite directions. The t-test says the south orchard has significantly more nitrate on average, because eight very high readings raise its mean. The Wilcox test says north samples tend to be higher, because 22 of the 30 south samples sit below every north sample. Neither test is wrong. They are answering different questions, and a plain plot of each data points shows which question matters for the data at hand: here, whether the concern is the total nitrate load (the mean) or the condition of a typical bed (the ranks).

## more than two means {-}

In the previous section we compared two means. What if we want to compare means from more than two study subjects? The first step is again to determine which tests to use. Let's consider our hawaii aquifer data again, though this time let's use all the aquifers, not just two:

```{r, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4.5, fig.cap = "Potassium in all ten Hawaiian aquifers. Boxplots of potassium abundance (x axis) for each aquifer (y axis), with each maroon point one measurement from a well drawing on that aquifer. The number of measurements ranges from three (aquifers 3 and 8) to thirty-three (aquifer 9). Data are from the 'hawaii_aquifers' dataset used in UMD CHEM5725."}
K_data <- hawaii_aquifers %>%
  filter(analyte == "K")

K_data

ggplot(data = K_data, aes(y = aquifer_code, x = abundance)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_point(color = "maroon", alpha = 0.6, size = 3)
```

Let's check visually to see if each group is normally distributed:

```{r, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 5, fig.cap = "Distributions of potassium in each of the ten Hawaiian aquifers. Histograms (gray bars, 30 bins) of potassium abundance (x axis), one panel per aquifer, in which the height of each bar is the number of measurements in that bin. A density curve (blue line) is drawn over each histogram, multiplied by ten so that it shares the y axis with the bars, which is why that axis is labeled density * 10. Aquifers with only a few measurements give histograms too sparse to judge normality by eye. Data are from the 'hawaii_aquifers' dataset used in UMD CHEM5725."}
K_data %>%
  group_by(aquifer_code) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = abundance)) +
    geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
    facet_wrap(~aquifer_code) +
    geom_density(aes(y = ..density..*10), colour = "blue")
```

Again, it is somewhat hard to tell visually if these data are normally distributed, so let's check with the Shapiro test. Don't forget: with the Shapiro test, we are looking within each group and so need to `group_by()`:

```{r}
K_data %>%
  group_by(aquifer_code) %>%
  shapiroTest(abundance)
```

Based on this test, it looks like the data for aquifer 9 is significantly different from a normal distribution (Shapiro test p < 0.05), while the other nine aquifers are not.

With more than two groups, running a separate t-test on every pair would multiply the chances of a false positive. Ten aquifers make 45 pairs, and at a 0.05 threshold about two of those 45 would come out significant by chance alone even if no aquifer differed from any other. The tests below compare every pair at once and correct the p-values for the number of comparisons made. (An ANOVA is often run first, to ask whether any group differs at all. It is not needed before the Games-Howell test, which makes its own correction. ANOVA answers other questions too, such as how two factors combine, and it has a chapter of its own.)

#### concept check {-}

Ten aquifers make 45 pairs. Fill in the blank so the table works that number out from the count of groups (each group pairs with every other group, and each pair is counted twice), then press Run.

<div class="webr-cell"><textarea class="webr-code">K_data %>%
  summarize(groups = n_distinct(aquifer_code)) %>%
  mutate(pairs = groups * (groups - 1) / ____)</textarea></div>

<div class="selfcheck" data-answer="2" data-explain="Ten aquifers make 45 pairs. Each separate t-test at a 0.05 threshold has a 5% chance of a false positive, so across 45 of them about two would come out significant by chance alone even if no aquifer differed from any other. The Games-Howell and Dunn tests compare every pair at once and correct the p values for the number of comparisons.">
<p class="scq">Self-check: Why compare the ten aquifers with a Games-Howell or Dunn test rather than a separate t-test on each of the 45 pairs?</p>
<label><input type="radio"> A t-test can only be run on aquifers with more than ten measurements</label>
<label><input type="radio"> The Games-Howell and Dunn tests do not need the data to be checked first</label>

</div>

<hr>

### Games-Howell test {-}

Let's assume for a second that every group passed the Shapiro test. This means that we could reasonably model our data with normal distributions and use a parametric test. For that we use the Games-Howell test (implemented using `gamesHowellTest`). This will essentially run a t-test on all the pairs of study subjects that we can derive from our data set (in this example, aquifer_1 vs. aquifer_2, aquifer_1 vs. aquifer_3, etc.). Like Welch's t-test, it compares each pair using those two groups' own spreads, rather than one spread shared by all the groups, so it needs no check that the groups have similar variances. After that, it will correct the p-values according to the number of comparisons that it performed. This controls the rate of type I error that we can expect from the test. These corrected values are provided to us in the `p.adj` column.

```{r}
K_data %>%
  gamesHowellTest(abundance ~ aquifer_code)
```

Using the output from our Games-Howell test, we can determine which means are similar. We can do this using the pGroups function:

```{r, message = FALSE}
groups_based_on_games_howell <- K_data %>%
  gamesHowellTest(abundance ~ aquifer_code) %>%
  pGroups()
groups_based_on_games_howell
```

We can use the output from `pGroups` to annotate our plot:

```{r, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4.5, fig.cap = "Potassium in the ten Hawaiian aquifers, labeled by Games-Howell test groups. Boxplots of potassium abundance (x axis) for each aquifer (y axis), with each maroon point one measurement from a well. The letters at the right come from a Games-Howell test on all 45 pairs of aquifers: aquifers that share a letter do not differ significantly (adjusted p > 0.05), and aquifers with no letter in common do. Data are from the 'hawaii_aquifers' dataset used in UMD CHEM5725."}
ggplot(data = K_data, aes(y = aquifer_code, x = abundance)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_point(color = "maroon", alpha = 0.6, size = 3) +
  geom_text(data = groups_based_on_games_howell, aes(y = treatment, x = 9, label = group))
```

Excellent! This plot shows us, using the letters on the same line with each aquifer, which means are the same and which are different. If a letter is shared among the labels in line with two aquifers, it means that their means do not differ significantly. For example, aquifer 2 ("af") and aquifer 6 ("abf") share the letters "a" and "f", so their means do not differ significantly. Aquifer 4 ("c") and aquifer 6 share no letter, so their means do differ. Because each pair is judged on its own two spreads, aquifers whose wells agree closely, such as aquifers 4 and 5, can be told apart from others by small differences in mean, while aquifer 10, whose seven wells scatter widely, shares a letter with every other aquifer.

<hr>

### Dunn test {-}

The above Games-Howell example is great, but remember - aquifer 9 did not pass the Shapiro test, so the Games-Howell test's p-values may not be accurate here, and a rank test is the more trustworthy choice. The rank-based counterpart of the Games-Howell test is the Dunn test. It pools every value from every group, ranks them all together, compares each pair's average rank within that single ranking, and then corrects the p-values for the number of comparisons. Everything said above about what the Wilcox test compares applies here too. Because the ranking is shared, the Dunn test and a pairwise Wilcox test can give slightly different answers for the same pair: with the Dunn test, a pair's ranks depend on which other groups are in the pool. (That shared ranking is the one the Kruskal test uses. The Kruskal test is the rank-based cousin of the ANOVA, and it appears in the ANOVA chapter.) Let's try:

```{r}
K_data %>%
  dunnTest(abundance ~ aquifer_code)
```

This gives us adjusted p-values for all pairwise comparisons. Once again, we can use `pGroups()` to give us a compact letter display for each group, which can then be used to annotate the plot:

```{r, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4.5, fig.cap = "Potassium in the ten Hawaiian aquifers, labeled by Dunn test groups. Boxplots of potassium abundance (x axis) for each aquifer (y axis), with each black point one measurement from a well. The letters at the right come from a Dunn test, a rank-based comparison of all 45 pairs of aquifers: aquifers that share a letter do not differ significantly (adjusted p > 0.05), and aquifers with no letter in common do. Data are from the 'hawaii_aquifers' dataset used in UMD CHEM5725."}
groups_based_on_dunn <- K_data %>%
  dunnTest(abundance ~ aquifer_code) %>%
  pGroups()
groups_based_on_dunn

ggplot(data = K_data, aes(y = aquifer_code, x = abundance)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_point(color = "black", alpha = 0.4, size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(name = "Potassium abundance", breaks = seq(0,10,1)) +
  scale_y_discrete(name = "Aquifer code") +
  geom_text(data = groups_based_on_dunn, aes(y = treatment, x = 9, label = group)) +
  theme_bw()
```

Note that these groupings are different from those generated by the Games-Howell test.

#### concept check {-}

Fill in the blank with the rank-based counterpart of the Games-Howell test, then press Run.

<div class="webr-cell"><textarea class="webr-code">K_data %>%
  ____(abundance ~ aquifer_code) %>%
  filter(p.adj < 0.05)</textarea></div>

<div class="selfcheck" data-answer="0" data-explain="Aquifer 9 failed the Shapiro test. The Games-Howell test does not need the groups to have similar spreads, but it does model each group with a normal distribution, so its p values may be inaccurate here. The Dunn test works on ranks, so it does not need that assumption. Here it finds 6 significantly different pairs where the Games-Howell test found 16.">
<p class="scq">Self-check: Why is the Dunn result the one to trust for these potassium data?</p>
<label><input type="radio"> Aquifer 9 is not normally distributed, so the Games-Howell test's assumption of normal groups does not hold</label>
<label><input type="radio"> The Dunn test always finds fewer significant pairs, so it is the safer choice</label>
<label><input type="radio"> The Dunn test does not need its p values corrected for the number of comparisons</label>
</div>

<hr>

## pairs of means {-}

Oftentimes we have more than two means to compare, but rather than wanting to compare all means at once, we want to compare them in a pairwise fashion. For example, suppose we want to know if any of the aquifers contain different amounts of Na and Cl. We are not interested in testing for differences among *all* values of Na and Cl, rather, we want to test all *pairs* of Na and Cl values arising from each aquifer. That is to say, we want to compare the means in each facet of the plot below:

```{r, fig.width = 11, fig.height = 4, fig.cap = "Sodium and chloride in each of the ten Hawaiian aquifers. Violin plots of abundance (y axis) for chloride and sodium (x axis), one panel per aquifer; each violin shows the distribution of one analyte in one aquifer and each point is one measurement from a well. The comparison of interest is the pair of violins within each panel, not the panels against each other. Data are from the 'hawaii_aquifers' dataset used in UMD CHEM5725."}
hawaii_aquifers %>%
  filter(analyte %in% c("Na", "Cl")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = analyte, y = abundance)) + geom_violin() + geom_point() + facet_grid(.~aquifer_code)
```

Fortunately, we can use an approach that is very similar to what we've learned in the earlier portions of this chapter, just with minor modifications. Let's have a look! We start with the Shapiro test, as usual (note that we group using two variables so that each analyte within each aquifer is considered as an individual distribution):

```{r}
hawaii_aquifers %>%
  filter(analyte %in% c("Na", "Cl")) %>%
  group_by(analyte, aquifer_code) %>%
  shapiroTest(abundance)
```

Looks like some of those distributions are significantly different from normal! So we need to be using non-parametric testing. If this were a simple case of two means we would use `wilcoxTest`, but we have many pairs, so we will use `pairwiseWilcoxTest` (note that with this test there are options for various styles of controlling for multiple comparisons, see: `?rstatix::pairwise_wilcox_test`):

```{r}
hawaii_aquifers %>%
  filter(analyte %in% c("Na", "Cl")) %>%
  group_by(aquifer_code) %>%
  pairwiseWilcoxTest(abundance~analyte)
```

Excellent! It looks like there is a statistically significant difference between the means of the abundances of Cl and Na in aquifer_2 and (surprisingly?) in aquifer_9 (perhaps due to the large number of observations?).

What would we have done if every distribution had passed the Shapiro test? Well, a `pairwiseTTest` of course! Like `tTest`, it runs Welch's t-test for each pair, so it needs no check that the two analytes have similar variances:

```{r}
hawaii_aquifers %>%
  filter(analyte %in% c("Na", "Cl")) %>%
  group_by(aquifer_code) %>%
  pairwiseTTest(abundance~analyte) -> test_output
  test_output
```

When the data are grouped, as they are here, `pairwiseTTest` and `pairwiseWilcoxTest` correct for multiple comparisons across all of the groups at once. Here there is one comparison per aquifer, ten in all, so the `p.adj` column holds Holm-adjusted p-values for the full set of ten comparisons, while the `p` column holds the uncorrected values. Read `p.adj` (and its stars, `p.adj.signif`) when deciding which differences are significant.

Excellent, now we see how to run parametric and non-parametric pairwise comparisons. How do we annotate plots with the output of these tests? Here is an example:

```{r, fig.width = 11, fig.height = 5, fig.cap = "Sodium and chloride in each of the ten Hawaiian aquifers, annotated with pairwise t-test results. Violin plots (gold) of abundance (y axis) for chloride and sodium (x axis), one panel per aquifer, with each maroon point one measurement from a well. The bracket in each panel joins the two analytes compared, and its label gives the significance of a pairwise t-test with Holm-adjusted p values across all ten aquifers: ns means p > 0.05, and one, two, three or four stars mean p < 0.05, 0.01, 0.001 or 0.0001. Data are from the 'hawaii_aquifers' dataset used in UMD CHEM5725."}

anno <- data.frame(
  xmin = test_output$group1,
  xmax = test_output$group2,
  y_position = c(150, 150, 150, 175, 80, 50, 300, 150, 50, 125),
  text = test_output$p.adj.signif,
  text_size = 10,
  text_vert_offset = 10,
  text_horiz_offset = 1.5,
  tip_length_xmin = 5,
  tip_length_xmax = 5,
  aquifer_code = test_output$aquifer_code,
  hjust = 0.5,
  vjust = 0.5
)

hawaii_aquifers %>%
  filter(analyte %in% c("Na", "Cl")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = analyte, y = abundance)) +
  geom_violin(fill = "gold", color = "black") +
  geom_point(shape = 21, fill = "maroon", color = "black") +
  facet_grid(.~aquifer_code) +
  geomSignif(data = anno, orientation = "horizontal") +
  scale_x_discrete(name = "Analyte") +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Abundance") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    text = element_text(size = 16)
    )

```

#### concept check {-}

Fill in the blank with the column that splits the data into one sodium-versus-chloride comparison per aquifer, then press Run.

<div class="webr-cell"><textarea class="webr-code">hawaii_aquifers %>%

  group_by(____) %>%
  pairwiseTTest(abundance ~ analyte) %>%
  select(aquifer_code, p, p.adj, p.adj.signif)</textarea></div>

Running ten tests gives ten chances of a false positive, and p.adj accounts for that. Aquifer 2 is the one aquifer whose p.adj is still below 0.05.">

<label><input type="radio"> Because p.adj compares sodium and chloride across every aquifer pooled together</label>
<label><input type="radio"> Because p.adj is corrected for the ten comparisons made, one per aquifer</label>
</div>

## chapter summary {-}

[Download this summary as a one-page PDF](https://thebustalab.github.io/integrated_bioanalytics/summary_sheets/11_comparing_means.pdf){.summary-pdf target="_blank"}

Before choosing a statistical test, look at the distribution of the data in each group. **Can each group be modeled by a normal distribution?** Check with the Shapiro test within each group. If they are not significantly different from normal, use a parametric test. If they are, use a rank test, which asks whether values in one group tend to be higher than values in the other. **How many groups are being compared?** With more than two, a separate t-test on every pair multiplies the chance of a false positive, so the Games-Howell and Dunn tests compare every pair at once and correct the p-values (read `p.adj`). The t-test used in this book is Welch's, and the Games-Howell test and `pairwiseTTest` likewise judge each pair on its own two spreads, so no test in this chapter needs a check for equal variances. The *p* value is the likelihood of getting data as extreme as the data in hand if the distributions they are coming from are in fact the same. The *p* value is not the probability that a detected difference is a false positive. Choosing a test comes down to how many groups are compared and whether the data are normal. Note that ANOVA is addressed in a separate, dedicated chapter.

| Function | What it is for | How it is used in this chapter |
|---|---|---|
| `shapiroTest(abundance)` | is each group roughly normal? (p > 0.05 means not significantly different from normal) | after `group_by()` on the grouping column(s) |
| `tTest(abundance ~ aquifer_code)` | two groups, roughly normal (Welch's t-test) | `response ~ predictor` formula |
| `wilcoxTest(abundance ~ aquifer_code)` | two groups, not normal (rank test) | `response ~ predictor` formula |
| `gamesHowellTest(abundance ~ aquifer_code)` | more than two groups, every pair, roughly normal (each pair judged on its own spreads) | read `p.adj` |
| `dunnTest(abundance ~ aquifer_code)` | more than two groups, every pair, rank-based | read `p.adj` |
| `pGroups()` | letters for each group from Games-Howell or Dunn output (a shared letter means no significant difference) | piped after `gamesHowellTest` or `dunnTest`, then drawn with `geom_text()` |
| `pairwiseTTest(abundance ~ analyte)`, `pairwiseWilcoxTest(abundance ~ analyte)` | one comparison within each of several groups | after `group_by(aquifer_code)`, with `p.adj` corrected across all the groups |
| `geomSignif()` | draws brackets and stars from pairwise test output | `data =` a table built from the test output |

## further reading {-}

- [One-Way ANOVA in R: Compare Group Means](https://www.datanovia.com/learn/biostatistics/anova/anova-in-r). When the data meet a stricter criterion, a little extra statistical power is available. If the groups' spreads are known to be similar, for example from a plot or from experience with the measurement method, the Tukey test, which pools the spread of all the groups into one estimate, detects real differences somewhat more often than the Games-Howell test. Datanovia's lesson shows the Tukey test alongside the Levene test, the usual check for equal variances, and the Games-Howell test for when the spreads differ. Keep in mind that with the three to five samples per group common in laboratory work, the Levene test rarely detects spreads that really are unequal, so passing it is weak evidence that the spreads are similar.

- [Parametric vs. Nonparametric Tests](https://statisticsbyjim.com/hypothesis-testing/nonparametric-parametric-tests/). Jim Frost breaks down when parametric tests are appropriate, the trade-offs of switching to rank-based alternatives, and how violation of assumptions affects power and interpretation.

- [The p value wars](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00259-019-04467-5). A short commentary by Ulrich Dirnagl capturing the ongoing debates about redefining statistical significance, the historical context of *p* < 0.05, and the risks of rigid thresholds versus broader inferential thinking.

- [Common statistical mistakes in biomedical research](https://elifesciences.org/articles/48175). The authors catalog frequent errors such as double dipping, underpowered designs, and misreported effect sizes, pairing each with pragmatic fixes for both authors and reviewers.

- [Wolfgang Huber on tiny *p*-values](https://www.cell.com/cell-systems/fulltext/S2405-4712(19)30071-7?_returnURL=https%3A%2F%2Flinkinghub.elsevier.com%2Fretrieve%2Fpii%2FS2405471219300717%3Fshowall%3Dtrue). Huber explains why extremely small *p*-values emerge in high-throughput experiments, how to think about multiplicity and effect sizes, and what to report alongside adjusted significance.
